title: Protocol Modifications for the DNS Security Extensions
subtitle: The rules that make signed DNS data servable, cacheable and checkable, from zone signing to the chain of trust.
summary: RFC 4035 is the protocol half of DNSSEC. It defines what a signed zone must contain, how authoritative servers add signatures and proofs to their answers, and how a validating resolver checks them. It restates the use of two header bits, AD and CD, and relies on the EDNS DO bit as the signal that a client wants DNSSEC data. It obsoletes the earlier RFC 2535 design and, with RFC 4033 and RFC 4034, forms the core DNSSEC specification.

eli5.summary: Every answer from the internet's phone book gets a wax seal, and a seal on the town's list vouches for each neighborhood's seal below it. This document says how to stamp the seals and how to check them, all the way up to a seal you already trust.

tldr.problem: Plain DNS answers can be forged, and the original DNSSEC design (RFC 2535) had grown into a patchwork of later fixes.
tldr.mechanism: Zones are signed with RRSIG records, parents vouch for child keys with DS records, NSEC records prove that names and types are absent, and validating resolvers walk the chain from a trust anchor using the DO, CD and AD header bits.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers can detect forged or altered DNS data. It is the base on which the signed root and many signed top-level domains operate, with later RFCs refining denial of existence and algorithms.

today: DNSSEC as specified here is in production use: the DNS root zone is signed, and a large share of top-level domains are signed. Validating recursive resolvers such as BIND, Unbound, Knot Resolver and PowerDNS Recursor implement the validation rules, and public resolvers such as 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 validate by default. The text has been refined rather than replaced: RFC 6840 collects clarifications and implementation notes, RFC 5155 adds NSEC3 as a hashed form of denial of existence, RFC 8198 allows aggressive use of validated NSEC records, and RFC 9364 (BCP 237) designates the DNSSEC family of documents as a Best Current Practice. Browsers and applications mostly rely on their resolver rather than validating themselves.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DNSSEC is a collection of new resource records and protocol modifications that add data origin authentication and data integrity to the DNS. RFC 4035 is the part that defines the protocol modifications. It sits in a family of three documents that "should be read together as a set": RFC 4033 gives the introduction and terminology, RFC 4034 defines the resource records, and this RFC defines how they are used.

The document is organised around the actors in a DNS lookup. Section 2 says what a signed zone must contain. Section 3 says how name servers behave when they serve one. Section 4 says how resolvers behave, and Section 5 says how a resolver uses the DNSSEC records to authenticate a response.

DNSSEC authenticates and protects the integrity of DNS data. It does not encrypt anything, so it adds no confidentiality.

RFC 4035 obsoletes RFC 2535, the first DNSSEC design, and also obsoletes RFC 3008, 3090, 3445, 3655, 3658, 3755, 3757 and 3845, which had patched it. It updates RFC 1034, RFC 1035 and several other core DNS documents.
sections.eli5: The internet's phone book can be tricked into giving you a wrong number. This document is the rulebook for putting a tamper-proof seal on each entry and for checking the seal before you believe it.

sections.title: Zone Signing
sections.content:
A signed zone carries four kinds of DNSSEC records: DNSKEY, RRSIG, NSEC and, optionally, DS. A zone missing them is an unsigned zone.

The administrator generates key pairs and signs every authoritative RRset with the private keys. For each RRset there MUST be at least one RRSIG whose owner name, class, type covered, original TTL, labels count and signer's name match the RRset, and whose algorithm, signer's name and key tag identify a zone key DNSKEY at the zone apex. RRSIG records themselves are not signed, since that would create an infinite loop. The apex NS RRset MUST be signed, but the NS RRsets at delegation points and glue address records MUST NOT be.

Every owner name with authoritative data, or with a delegation NS RRset, MUST have an NSEC record, and its type bitmap must show both NSEC and RRSIG. A DS RRset SHOULD be present at a delegation when the child zone is signed, and DS RRsets MUST NOT appear at a zone's apex.

Two record types are allowed somewhere the original DNS forbade: NSEC and DS may sit on the parent side of a zone cut. RFC 1034 said only NS records could. Likewise the CNAME rule changes so that a CNAME can coexist with RRSIG and NSEC.
sections.eli5: Signing a zone is like putting a wax seal on every page of a book, and listing every page so nobody can quietly rip one out. The town hall also keeps a note saying which seal each neighborhood uses.

sections.title: Serving: Authoritative Name Servers
sections.content:
A security-aware name server MUST support EDNS0 (RFC 2671), MUST support a message size of at least 1220 octets, and SHOULD support 4000. It only adds DNSSEC data when the query has an EDNS OPT record with the DO bit set; otherwise it treats RRSIG, DNSKEY and NSEC as ordinary data.

When DO is set, an authoritative server for a signed zone includes RRSIG records with each signed RRset, in the same section, and MUST set the TC bit if the RRSIGs for the Answer or Authority sections do not fit. In a referral it includes the DS RRset and its RRSIG, or an NSEC record proving that no DS exists.

For negative answers it includes NSEC records in four cases: No Data, Name Error, Wildcard Answer and Wildcard No Data. Zone transfers (AXFR and IXFR) are unchanged by DNSSEC.

DO bit
Set by the client to ask for DNSSEC records. Without it, nothing changes.
Truncation
If required RRSIG or NSEC records do not fit, the server sets TC so the client retries.
DS lives in the parent
A DS query is answered by the parent zone, which needs special handling by servers that serve only the child.
sections.eli5: When you ask for the sealed version, the helper hands you the answer and the seal together. If the seal will not fit in the envelope, the helper says so and you ask again with a bigger one.

sections.title: Resolving and the AD and CD Bits
sections.content:
A security-aware resolver MUST send an EDNS OPT record with DO set, MUST support at least 1220 octets, SHOULD support 4000, and SHOULD validate every response unless the query had CD set, the application opted out, or local policy disables validation. It MUST be configurable with at least one trusted public key or DS record, called a trust anchor.

RFC 4035 gives the two new header bits clear owners. The CD (Checking Disabled) bit belongs to resolvers, and a server MUST copy it from query to response. The AD (Authentic Data) bit belongs to name servers, which MUST NOT set it unless all RRsets in the Answer and Authority sections are considered authentic. Servers MUST ignore AD in queries, and a resolver MUST clear it when sending one.

A resolver MAY keep a "BAD cache" of data that failed validation, but must assign it a TTL (which should be small) and should only answer from it after repeated failures, so it cannot amplify an attack. Stub resolvers need to understand DNSSEC records, but a validating stub SHOULD set CD and need not look at AD.
sections.eli5: You can tell the helper "I will check the seal myself, just hand it over" (CD). The helper can write on the envelope "I checked it and the seal is good" (AD), but you should only believe that note if you trust the delivery route.

sections.title: Secure, Insecure, Bogus, Indeterminate
sections.content:
A resolver must be able to tell four situations apart for any RRset. This is one of the most useful ideas in the RFC, because it separates "unsigned" from "broken."

An unsigned zone below a signed parent is not an attack: the parent proves there is no DS, and the child is simply insecure. A signed zone whose signatures fail is bogus, and the resolver should not return the data. If a resolver cannot reach DNSSEC-aware servers it cannot decide, and the status is indeterminate.

The RFC also covers islands of security, signed zones with no authentication chain from the parent. A validator that cannot obtain a key for such an island SHOULD behave as if the zones in it were unsigned. Importantly, "the absence of DNSSEC data in a response MUST NOT by itself be taken as an indication that no authentication information exists," because an attacker could strip it.
sections.eli5: A seal can be good, missing because the shop never uses seals, broken, or impossible to check because the road is closed. Each case needs a different reaction.

sections.title: Authenticating Responses
sections.content:
Validation begins at a trust anchor, a configured DNSKEY or DS record. The resolver first authenticates the zone's apex DNSKEY RRset: the configured key must appear in it and an RRSIG must verify the set. From there it can walk down by authenticating referrals with DS records.

A DS record identifies a child DNSKEY by algorithm and key tag, and carries a digest of that key. The child's DNSKEY set is accepted if the DS is authenticated by the parent's keys, the child key hashes to the DS digest, the key has the Zone Flag set, and its signature covers the child's apex DNSKEY RRset.

To check any RRset against an RRSIG, the resolver verifies that owner name, class, signer and type covered match, that the current time falls between the Inception and Expiration times, and that a matching zone key exists. It rebuilds the signed data from the RRSIG RDATA (without the signature) plus the canonical RRset, using the original TTL. If several DNSKEYs match it tries each. After success, the cached TTL is capped at the smallest of the received TTLs, the Original TTL, and the time left before signature expiry.

If no RRSIG validates, the response SHOULD be considered BAD. A recursive server then returns RCODE 2 (server failure), unless the query had CD set.
sections.eli5: You start from a seal you already trust, such as the national one. It vouches for the state's seal, which vouches for the town's, and so on down to the page you asked about. If any link breaks, you do not trust the page.

sections.title: Authenticated Denial of Existence
sections.content:
Signing what exists is not enough: an attacker could forge a "no such name" answer. DNSSEC therefore signs a chain of NSEC records, each listing an existing name, the next name in canonical order and the record types present at the name. If the requested name falls between an NSEC owner name and its Next Domain Name, the name does not exist.

Because a wildcard might have matched, a proof of non-existence must also show that no wildcard RRset could have produced an answer. That can take more than one NSEC record, and a resolver that does not get them all, perhaps because of truncation, MUST resend the query while still bounding its work.

For wildcard-expanded answers, an RRSIG with a Labels value smaller than the owner name's label count shows expansion. The validator verifies the signature as for the wildcard name and then checks that no exact match or closer wildcard exists.

At a delegation there are two NSEC sets, one in the parent and one in the child. They are told apart because only the child's NSEC lists SOA, and the resolver MUST use the parent's when proving that a DS set does not exist.
sections.eli5: To prove there is no page 12, the book shows a sealed note: "after page 11 comes page 13." The note also has to say there is no hidden page that could count as 12.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short and focuses on the new header bits. An active attacker who can set the CD bit in a query, or the AD bit in a response, can defeat the protection that DNSSEC offers to security-oblivious recursive resolvers. For that reason, use of these bits by a recursive resolver requires a secure channel. A resolver MUST disregard CD and AD in a response unless it came over a secure channel or the resolver was explicitly configured to trust the bits.

The RFC also warns that facilities for stub resolvers may be inadequate, because recovery from validation failure is application-specific. Operators of recursive servers must choose a local validation policy carefully, since a wrong choice could accidentally deny service to the clients they support.

General security considerations are in RFC 4033, and those specific to the record types are in RFC 4034. IANA considerations are minor: no new header bits are defined, since the CD and AD bits were already reserved by RFC 2535.
sections.eli5: A note that says "already checked" is only worth trusting if nobody could have scribbled it on the way. So you only trust those notes when you know the road is safe.

items.title: DNSKEY at the apex
items.text: The zone's public keys. At least one is needed as a secure entry point if the zone is not an island of security.

items.title: RRSIG on every authoritative RRset
items.text: Not on delegation NS records, glue, or other RRSIG records.

items.title: NSEC on every name
items.text: Every name with authoritative data or a delegation, chained in canonical order.

items.title: DS in the parent
items.text: A digest of the child's key, stored on the parent side of the zone cut, never at an apex.

cells: DO (in EDNS OPT)
Resolver, in queries
"Send me the DNSSEC records."
Servers add RRSIG, NSEC and DS only when it is set
CD
Resolver, in queries
"Checking disabled: I will validate myself."
Server MUST copy it into the response
AD
Name server, in responses
"All Answer and Authority data is authentic."
Ignored in queries; resolver clears it when sending

items.title: Secure
items.text: A chain of signed DNSKEY and DS records links a trusted anchor to the RRset, and it validates.

items.title: Insecure
items.text: The resolver knows there is no chain from any trusted starting point, for example an unsigned zone.

items.title: Bogus
items.text: The resolver ought to be able to build a chain but cannot, from failed signatures or missing data.

items.title: Indeterminate
items.text: The resolver cannot tell whether the RRset should be signed, because it cannot reach the needed servers.

data.title: Signed data reconstruction
data.code:
signed_data = RRSIG_RDATA | RR(1) | RR(2)...

RR(i) = name | type | class | OrigTTL | RDATA length | RDATA

  RRSIG_RDATA excludes the Signature field.
  OrigTTL is taken from the RRSIG Original TTL field.
  The set of all RR(i) is sorted into canonical order.
